title: Hallucinations in Bibliographic Recommendation: Citation Frequency as a Proxy for Training Data Redundancy
topic: LLM bibliographic hallucination and citation frequency
data_source: GPT-4.1 API; Google Scholar; Sentence-BERT validation
method: synthetic LLM experiment; manual validation; t-test; correlation; logistic regression
key_variables: citation count; factual score; cosine similarity between generated and authentic metadata; topic domain
key_findings: GPT-4.1 generated 100 records across 20 CS topics; highly cited papers had higher factual scores; log citation count correlated strongly with metadata fidelity; around 1000 citations marked near-verbatim memorization.
limitations: Only GPT-4.1; only CS; only 100 generated records; citation count is a proxy for training redundancy; no real human citation behavior.
relevance_to_our_project: high - directly links citation frequency to LLM recall and Matthew-effect mechanism
notes: Seed extraction: RQ asks whether citation frequency predicts hallucinated references. Core hypothesis: highly cited papers are more likely to be memorized/recalled. Claimed contribution: redundancy/memorization threshold for bibliographic recommendation.

title: ChatGPT cites the most-cited articles and journals, relying solely on Google Scholar's citation counts. As a result, AI may amplify the Matthew Effect in environmental science
topic: ChatGPT citation selection and Matthew Effect
data_source: ChatGPT-4 prompts; Google Scholar citation counts
key_variables: ChatGPT-generated references; Google Scholar citation counts; publication year; journal
key_findings: ChatGPT-generated environmental-science review introductions cited highly cited and older papers; median cited reference count was 1184.5; Nature was the most cited journal.
limitations: Prompt sensitivity; early GPT version; one broad field; no control for relevance or validity; no real citation data.
relevance_to_our_project: high - early direct Matthew Effect evidence
notes: Seed extraction: RQ asks whether ChatGPT predominantly cites highly cited environmental-science publications. Hypothesis: ChatGPT citation generation inherits Google Scholar-like cumulative advantage.

title: Who Gets Seen in the Age of AI? Adoption Patterns of Large Language Models in Scholarly Writing and Citation Outcomes
topic: AI-assisted writing, visibility, regional citation flows
data_source: Scopus; SJR; Binoculars zero-shot AI detector
level_of_analysis: paper level; region/country level; network level
method: zero-inflated negative binomial regression; logistic/OLS adoption models; pre/post ChatGPT; network analysis
key_variables: AI-likeness/humanness; Post-GPT and model-release dummies; citations; cross-region citations; journal tier; PageRank; betweenness; conductance; assortativity
key_findings: Analyzes 238218 Scopus CS articles from Jan 2021-Jan 2025. Global East shows stronger AI-likeness adoption; AI-adaptive writing is associated with citation visibility; country-level networks show modest Eastward visibility gains but stronger intra-regional clustering.
limitations: Observational network analysis; quasi-instrument assumptions are weak; pagination/sampling limits; AI detectors may penalize Global East writing; no lead-lag/event-study validation.
relevance_to_our_project: high - closest seed to real-world temporal network and democratization question
gap_category: real-world behavior; temporal network evolution; causal inference; democratization
notes: Seed extraction: RQs cover regional AI adoption, visibility outcomes, and citation-network structure after ChatGPT. Claimed contribution: links writing-style AI-likeness to visibility and global citation-network shifts. Studies correlation plus partial causal argument, not clean causality.

title: How Deep Do Large Language Models Internalize Scientific Literature and Citation Practices?
topic: LLM-generated references across science and citation-practice internalization
data_source: SciSciNet; GPT-4o; fuzzy matching; embeddings; citation graphs
level_of_analysis: citation level; paper level; field level; network level
method: large synthetic LLM experiment; bibliometric matching; Wilcoxon tests; embedding similarity; graph analysis
key_variables: citation counts; existence rate; title length; author count; publication year; self-citation; embedding similarity; citation graph measures
key_findings: GPT-4o generated 274951 references for 10000 Q1 papers. Existing generated references had higher citation counts than ground truth across fields and years; generated references were semantically relevant, more recent, shorter-titled, had fewer authors, and reduced self-citations.
limitations: Controlled setting without interactive prompting or external databases; parametric-only focus excludes RAG/tool use; generated references are not real human final citations.
relevance_to_our_project: high - large-scale evidence that LLMs reinforce Matthew Effect while preserving relevance
gap_category: Matthew Effect; synthetic behavior; RAG/tool augmentation
notes: Seed extraction: RQ asks how LLM reference suggestions align with human citation practices across domains. Hypothesis: LLMs may amplify established citation patterns. Contribution: large cross-field synthetic benchmark.

title: Large Language Models Reflect Human Citation Patterns with a Heightened Citation Bias
topic: LLM citation bias versus human citation patterns
data_source: arXiv papers; Semantic Scholar; GPT-4; GPT-4o; Claude 3.5
level_of_analysis: citation level; paper level; network level
method: synthetic LLM experiment; controlled generation; Semantic Scholar verification; nonparametric tests; citation graph analysis
key_variables: generated references; ground-truth references; citation count; publication year; title length; authors; venue; network embedding
key_findings: For 166 AAAI/NeurIPS/ICML/ICLR papers, LLM-generated references resembled human patterns but showed stronger high-citation bias after controls. The bias held for GPT-4, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5; generated references were embedded in relevant citation networks.
limitations: Only ML papers; controlled prompts; excludes search and RAG; does not measure real human LLM-assisted writing or downstream citation network evolution.
relevance_to_our_project: high - core seed for Matthew Effect versus LLM citation bias
gap_category: Matthew Effect; synthetic behavior; RAG/tool augmentation
notes: Seed extraction: RQ asks whether parametric LLMs reproduce or amplify human citation patterns. Contribution: controlled comparison of LLM and human references with graph-level plausibility evidence.

title: Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT
authors: William H. Walters and Esther Isabelle Wilder
topic: ChatGPT citation fabrication and bibliographic accuracy
data_source: ChatGPT-3.5; ChatGPT-4; 42 multidisciplinary topics
key_variables: fabricated citation rate; citation metadata error rate; model version
key_findings: Generated 636 citations in 84 short papers. GPT-4 improved over GPT-3.5 but fabricated and inaccurate references remained common.
limitations: Focuses accuracy/existence rather than bias, relevance, citation prestige, or real-world adoption.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - important baseline for hallucination but less about citation inequality
notes: Backward foundational for LLM-generated reference reliability.

title: Exploring the Boundaries of Reality: Investigating the Phenomenon of Artificial Intelligence Hallucination in Scientific Writing Through ChatGPT References
topic: ChatGPT hallucinated scientific references
data_source: ChatGPT-generated scientific writing references
method: synthetic LLM experiment; manual reference checking
key_variables: existence and accuracy of generated references
key_findings: Finds ChatGPT can generate plausible but false references in scientific writing contexts.
limitations: Small and domain-specific; mostly reliability rather than visibility or network effects.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - supports hallucination/training-coverage mechanism
notes: Cited by P003 as early hallucination evidence.

title: ChatGPT Hallucinates Non-existent Citations: Evidence from Economics
venue: Journal of Economics and Finance Education
topic: LLM citation hallucination in economics
data_source: ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 prompts based on Journal of Economic Literature topics
key_variables: fabricated citation rate; model version; economics topic
key_findings: ChatGPT summarized economics concepts but cited non-existent references; over 30% of GPT-3.5 citations did not exist and GPT-4 only slightly reduced the rate.
limitations: Education/economics setting; not about citation bias, author prestige, or real-world citation outcomes.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - useful business-adjacent evidence of citation reliability but not network impact
notes: Shows business/economics-related venues have studied hallucinated citations, but not the full Matthew/democratization question.

title: How well do LLMs cite relevant medical references? An evaluation framework and analyses
topic: LLM source support and RAG medical references
data_source: Generated medical QA; SourceCheckup; GPT-4 with and without RAG
key_variables: statement support by cited source; response support; model and RAG condition
key_findings: Evaluates whether generated medical references support claims; even GPT-4 with RAG left about 30% of individual statements unsupported and nearly half of responses not fully supported.
limitations: Medical QA rather than academic citation choice; support checking not citation network inequality.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - directly informs RAG/tool gap and citation trustworthiness
notes: Evidence that RAG improves grounding but does not solve citation support; not a study of citation prestige bias.

title: Quantifying large language model usage in scientific papers
topic: Population-level LLM usage in scientific writing
data_source: arXiv; bioRxiv; Nature Portfolio; corpus-level distributional estimation
method: statistical mixture/distributional quantification; temporal trend analysis
key_variables: estimated LLM-modified text share; field; time; author preprint frequency; topic crowdedness
key_findings: Across 950965 papers from Jan 2020-Feb 2024, LLM-modified writing rose after ChatGPT, fastest in CS and lower in math/Nature portfolio; LLM modification associated with crowded topics and shorter papers.
limitations: Measures writing style, not citations or impact; individual-level classification is avoided; no causal design.
relevance_to_our_project: high - establishes adoption heterogeneity needed for treatment intensity
notes: Backward evidence for AI adoption timing and field heterogeneity.

title: Is ChatGPT Transforming Academics' Writing Style?
topic: ChatGPT-style academic writing prevalence
data_source: One million arXiv abstracts; GPT-3.5 rewritten abstracts for calibration
key_variables: LLM-style word density; field; submission date
key_findings: Finds growing ChatGPT-style writing in arXiv abstracts, especially CS, with an estimated CS fraction around 35% under their GPT-3.5 revision baseline.
limitations: Writing-style proxy; not citation outcomes; arXiv only; model calibration assumptions.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - useful adoption proxy for temporal designs
notes: Backward evidence for post-ChatGPT writing-style shift.

title: Human-LLM Coevolution: Evidence from Academic Writing
topic: Human adaptation to LLM writing markers
data_source: arXiv abstracts; word-frequency analysis
key_variables: frequency of LLM-associated words; time; field
key_findings: Shows some words previously overused by ChatGPT declined after public attention, while others continued rising, suggesting human-LLM coevolution and detector instability.
limitations: Not about citation behavior; indicates measurement threats for AI-likeness proxies.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - important threat to validity for detector-based designs
notes: Highlights that AI-use proxies may change as authors adapt.

title: Have AI-Generated Texts from LLM Infiltrated the Realm of Scientific Writing? A Large-Scale Analysis of Preprint Platforms
topic: LLM-generated text in scientific preprints
data_source: Preprint platforms; Binoculars LLM-text detector
key_variables: AI-generated text likelihood; preprint platform; field; time; citations in follow-on discussions unclear
key_findings: Reported large-scale infiltration of AI-like text in preprint platforms and motivated later work connecting AI-likeness to visibility.
limitations: Detector-based and preprint-specific; not designed for citation network inequality.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - supports adoption measurement and detector concerns
notes: Referenced by P003 as a prevalence study.

title: The Impact of Large Language Models on Language Proficiencies in Scientific Publications
authors: Yafei Liang, Tianxi Yang and Feng Zhu
topic: LLMs and language proficiency in scientific publications
data_source: SSRN metadata across seven subject areas
level_of_analysis: paper level; author language group; discipline level
key_variables: ChatGPT release; EFL versus non-EFL authors; language proficiency; discipline
key_findings: Uses ChatGPT 3.5 release in Nov 2022 as a natural experiment and reports larger post-release language-proficiency improvements for EFL-authored SSRN papers, especially social sciences.
limitations: Abstract-only proceedings record; focuses language proficiency, not citation behavior or networks; full controls unclear from available abstract.
relevance_to_our_project: high - business/management venue and causal design but not citation impact
notes: Strong evidence that business/management venues are beginning to study GenAI effects on scholarly writing with DID.

title: Do Large Language Models Inflate Scientific Impact? Evidence from Citation Patterns before and after 2022
authors: Sofiia Paklina, Petr Parshakov and Elena Rapoport
topic: LLM-assisted writing and citation impact
data_source: arXiv records plus Crossref bibliometrics; trained AI-writing classifier
method: regression with rich controls and fixed effects; counterfactual machine learning
key_variables: predicted LLM-assisted writing; citations; journal characteristics; collaboration size; reference lists; abstract length; authors' prior citation records
key_findings: Finds papers with abstracts showing LLM-assisted writing receive more citations than otherwise similar papers and above counterfactual pre-2022 predictions.
limitations: Preprint; AI-use detection may be noisy; not a clean exogenous treatment; arXiv/Crossref scope; mechanisms not fully isolated.
relevance_to_our_project: high - directly tests real-world citation impact after GenAI adoption
gap_category: real-world behavior; causal inference; Matthew Effect
notes: A near match to the proposed real-world citation-impact idea, so novelty must be narrowed beyond citation premium alone.

title: Scientific production in the era of Large Language Models
topic: LLM adoption, productivity, research quality, and citation diversity
data_source: 2.1M preprints; 28K peer-review reports; 246M online accesses
level_of_analysis: author level; paper level; access/citation level
method: detected-adoption event study; large-scale observational analysis
key_variables: LLM adoption; paper production; writing complexity; paper quality; cited-work diversity; younger/less-cited cited documents
key_findings: Reports LLM adopters increase paper production and cite more diverse prior work, including younger and less-cited documents, suggesting possible democratization in real behavior.
limitations: Adoption timing based on detection can be mechanically linked to output; challenged by P017; observational and detector-dependent.
relevance_to_our_project: high - directly challenges simple Matthew-effect hypothesis
gap_category: real-world behavior; author-level; democratization; causal inference
notes: Important counterevidence: LLM use may diversify cited work in real-world author behavior.

title: Comment on Scientific production in the era of large language models
authors: Thomas Renault, Antonin Bergeaud and Clément Bosquet
topic: Validity critique of LLM-adoption event studies
data_source: Replication/simulation of Kusumegi et al. design
key_variables: first detected LLM-use month; output; placebo flags; pre-ChatGPT window
key_findings: Shows first-detection timing can mechanically create spurious positive post-treatment paths; placebo exercises produce similar event-study patterns.
limitations: Comment, not independent substantive effect estimate; focused on productivity design, not citation diversity directly.
relevance_to_our_project: high - crucial threat-to-validity evidence for causal designs
notes: Warns against naive event-study timing based on first AI-detected paper.

title: AI-assisted writing and the reorganization of scientific knowledge
topic: AI-assisted writing, disruption, and knowledge recombination
data_source: Approximately 2M full-text research articles; citation networks
level_of_analysis: paper level; author-field-year panel; network level
method: within-author within-field models; fixed effects; citation-network measures
key_variables: AI-assisted writing intensity; disruption; cross-field citation breadth; citation concentration; time period
key_findings: After 2023, AI-writing intensity is associated with more disruptive citation structures, but without broader cross-field sourcing; cross-field citation breadth association weakens.
limitations: Observational; AI-writing proxy; structural citation measures do not prove substantive novelty; not specifically Matthew vs democratization.
relevance_to_our_project: high - closest to temporal citation-network evolution after GenAI
gap_category: temporal network evolution; real-world behavior; causal inference
notes: Supports a refined gap on network evolution and recombination, not just citation counts.

title: Are ChatGPT and large language models 'the answer' to bringing us closer to systematic review automation?
topic: LLMs for systematic-review automation
data_source: ChatGPT examples and systematic-review workflow discussion
key_variables: review automation tasks; screening; extraction; writing support
key_findings: Argues LLMs may support systematic reviews but require caution, verification, and human oversight.
limitations: Not a citation-bias study; limited empirical citation data.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - shows early literature-review automation context
notes: Backward citation for citation/literature-review use cases.

title: Automating research synthesis with domain-specific large language model fine-tuning
topic: Fine-tuned LLMs for systematic literature review automation
data_source: Domain-specific LLM fine-tuning; source-tracking mechanisms
method: LLM system design; fine-tuning; source tracking
key_variables: hallucination mitigation; source traceability; review automation quality
key_findings: Proposes domain-specific fine-tuning and source tracking for automated research synthesis.
limitations: Focuses SLR workflow quality rather than citation prestige bias or real citation outcomes.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - relevant to tool-augmented citation behavior gap
notes: Shows tool/system work exists but not bias-oriented evaluation.

title: Generative artificial intelligence for literature reviews
topic: GenAI for literature reviews in IS/management research
data_source: Conceptual/methodological review
key_variables: literature-review tasks; epistemic risks; human oversight
key_findings: Provides business/IS-oriented guidance on GenAI for literature reviews and research synthesis.
limitations: Does not empirically test citation bias, Matthew Effect, or citation-network evolution.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - business/IS venue coverage exists but not the specific impact question
notes: Indicates the business venue gap is only open for citation-network impact, not for GenAI-literature-review methods generally.

title: Large Language Models as Tools for Integrative Reviews
topic: LLMs as tools for integrative management reviews
data_source: Management review methodology
key_variables: LLM use in integrative reviews; review quality; validity concerns
key_findings: Discusses how LLMs can assist integrative reviews in management scholarship.
limitations: Not empirical; no citation behavior, author visibility, or network design.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - business/management venue recognizes LLM review tools
notes: Business/management venues have entered the GenAI-review conversation but not the citation inequality question.

title: A context-aware citation recommendation model with BERT and graph convolutional networks
topic: Citation recommendation systems before LLMs
data_source: Citation contexts; BERT; graph convolutional networks
level_of_analysis: citation level; paper level; network level
method: citation recommendation model; neural embeddings; graph learning
key_variables: citation context; candidate paper relevance; graph structure
key_findings: Develops context-aware citation recommendation using text and graph information.
limitations: Pre-LLM; optimization target is recommendation accuracy, not fairness or downstream citation inequality.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - baseline for citation recommender/tool gap
notes: Important to distinguish LLM citation generation from older citation recommender literature.

title: Scholarly recommendation systems: a literature survey
topic: Survey of scholarly recommender systems
data_source: Scholarly recommender literature
key_variables: recommendation task types; datasets; evaluation metrics
key_findings: Surveys scholarly paper and citation recommendation systems and public datasets.
limitations: Not focused on GenAI adoption or citation inequality; fairness and Matthew Effect are not central.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - maps adjacent recommender-system landscape
notes: Useful for positioning tool-augmented citation behavior.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
topic: Retrieval-augmented generation foundation
data_source: Wikipedia/DPR retrieval; sequence-to-sequence generation benchmarks
key_variables: retrieved documents; generation quality; factual grounding
key_findings: Introduces RAG as a way to combine parametric and nonparametric memory for knowledge-intensive tasks.
limitations: Not about scholarly citation selection or bias; foundational only.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - foundation for RAG/tool-augmentation gap
notes: Needed to define RAG as a mechanism distinct from parametric LLM citation generation.

title: The Matthew Effect in Science
topic: Cumulative advantage and recognition inequality
data_source: Sociology of science theory
key_variables: scientific recognition; status; cumulative advantage
key_findings: Introduces Matthew Effect: eminent scientists receive disproportionate credit and recognition.
limitations: Classic theory, not AI-specific; no empirical LLM design.
relevance_to_our_project: high - conceptual foundation for proposed gap
notes: Foundational pre-2023 work necessary for framing.

title: Unpacking the Matthew Effect in Citations
topic: Matthew Effect in citation accumulation
data_source: Citation data
key_variables: prior citations; later citations; paper quality proxies
key_findings: Shows cumulative advantage in citations and attempts to separate quality from preferential attachment.
limitations: Pre-LLM; no GenAI; field/time scope depends on dataset.
relevance_to_our_project: high - empirical foundation for citation Matthew Effect
notes: Useful baseline for asking whether LLMs stabilize, weaken, or intensify cumulative advantage.

title: Electronic Publication and the Narrowing of Science and Scholarship
topic: Search/access technologies and narrowing of citations
data_source: Journal citation and online access data
level_of_analysis: citation level; journal level; field level
key_variables: online availability; citation concentration; age of cited work; breadth of citations
key_findings: Finds electronic access/search is associated with narrower and more recent citation patterns.
limitations: Pre-LLM; not causal in modern GenAI context.
relevance_to_our_project: high - analog for how discovery tools reshape citation breadth
notes: Useful historical analogy for search/RAG/LLM-mediated discovery.

title: Science of science
topic: Science of science overview
data_source: Cross-domain scientometrics literature
level_of_analysis: field level; network level; author level
key_variables: citation networks; careers; teams; innovation; impact
key_findings: Synthesizes mechanisms of scientific discovery, collaboration, citations, and impact.
limitations: Broad review; not LLM-specific.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - background for citation-network evolution and inequality mechanisms
notes: Foundational framing for network and author-level designs.

title: Science is shaped by Wikipedia: Evidence from a randomized control trial
authors: Neil C. Thompson and Douglas Hanley
topic: External knowledge platforms shaping scientific attention
data_source: Randomized Wikipedia article creation; scientific literature tracking
key_variables: Wikipedia exposure; scientific language; topic attention
key_findings: Shows Wikipedia can causally shape scientific language and attention, demonstrating that knowledge platforms can redirect research attention.
limitations: Not LLM-specific; Wikipedia intervention differs from AI writing tools.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - causal template for platform-mediated science visibility
notes: Useful for thinking about feasible causal designs around information-access shocks.

title: A systematic literature review of retrieval-augmented generation: techniques, metrics, and challenges
topic: RAG techniques and evaluation landscape
data_source: Citation-weighted PRISMA review of 128 RAG studies from 2020-May 2025
key_variables: RAG architecture; evaluation metrics; hallucination/factuality; retrieval design
key_findings: Synthesizes RAG techniques, metrics, and challenges; emphasizes grounding, retrieval, verification, and agentic controllers.
limitations: General RAG review, not scholarly citation bias; citation-weighted sampling may underrepresent emerging work.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - confirms RAG is heavily studied but citation-bias effects are not central
notes: Supports assessment that RAG/tool gap is open specifically for citation inequality, not for RAG methods generally.

title: Bibliometrics: The Leiden Manifesto for research metrics
topic: Responsible research metrics and evaluation principles
data_source: Research evaluation policy and bibliometrics
level_of_analysis: institution level; researcher level; field level
key_variables: research metrics; field normalization; qualitative judgment; transparency; systemic effects
key_findings: Proposes ten principles for responsible metrics, including supporting qualitative expert assessment, measuring against mission, protecting locally relevant research, using open/transparent data, accounting for field variation, and scrutinizing indicators regularly.
limitations: Not specific to citation behavior or LLMs; focused on assessment rather than citation generation.
relevance_to_our_project: high - supplies academic standard for responsible use of citation-based indicators
notes: Important for revising health standard: citation indicators should be contextual, transparent, field-aware, and reflexively monitored.

title: San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment
topic: Research assessment reform and misuse of journal metrics
data_source: Research assessment policy statement
level_of_analysis: researcher level; institution level; journal level
key_variables: journal impact factor; article-level metrics; primary literature; open reference lists; metric manipulation
key_findings: Argues against using journal-based metrics as surrogates for article or researcher quality; recommends judging scientific content directly, considering broader outputs, opening reference lists, citing primary literature, and resisting metric manipulation.
limitations: Declaration, not empirical paper; broad assessment focus.
relevance_to_our_project: high - directly informs what a healthy citation evaluation system should not do
gap_category: responsible metrics; system health; citation ethics
notes: Useful for defining health as content-based assessment rather than prestige proxy optimization.

title: The Metric Tide: Report of the Independent Review of the Role of Metrics in Research Assessment and Management
topic: Responsible metrics in research assessment
data_source: UK research assessment evidence review
level_of_analysis: institution level; policy level; field level
key_variables: robustness; humility; transparency; diversity; reflexivity; quantitative indicators
key_findings: Frames responsible metrics around robustness, humility, transparency, diversity, and reflexivity; argues metrics should support, not replace, expert judgment and should be monitored for systemic effects.
limitations: Policy report, not citation-behavior study; UK-centered.
relevance_to_our_project: high - provides a compact standard for citation system health and indicator governance
notes: Useful bridge between ecosystem health and measurement governance.

title: The Hong Kong Principles for assessing researchers: Fostering research integrity
topic: Researcher assessment and integrity-supporting incentives
data_source: World Conference on Research Integrity consultation; responsible research practice examples
level_of_analysis: researcher level; institution level; policy level
key_variables: responsible practices; transparent reporting; open science; replication; peer review; research integrity
key_findings: Argues assessment systems should reward rigorous, transparent, open, and responsible practices rather than only novelty or citation impact.
limitations: Not specific to citations or LLMs; more about researcher assessment incentives.
relevance_to_our_project: high - connects citation health to research-integrity incentives
gap_category: responsible metrics; system health; citation ethics
notes: Supports adding integrity and correctability to the health standard.

title: Citations, Citation Indicators, and Research Quality: An Overview of Basic Concepts and Theories
authors: Dag W. Aksnes, Liv Langfeldt and Paul Wouters
topic: Validity of citation indicators as research-quality measures
data_source: Scientometric literature
level_of_analysis: paper level; researcher level; institution level
key_variables: citations; scientific impact; plausibility; originality; societal value; research quality
key_findings: Concludes citations reflect aspects of scientific impact/relevance but not all dimensions of quality, such as solidity, originality, and societal value.
limitations: Review-level synthesis; not LLM-specific.
relevance_to_our_project: high - warns against equating citation allocation with true research quality
notes: Important for refining health: citation concentration is not automatically quality concentration.

title: What do citation counts measure? An updated review of studies on citations in scientific documents published between 2006 and 2018
topic: Citation motivations, contexts, functions and polarity
data_source: 41 studies of citation context/motivation from 2006-2018
key_variables: citation context; semantics; linguistic patterns; citation location; polarity; citation motivation
key_findings: Shows papers are cited for many scientific and non-scientific reasons; recommends analyzing citation context, semantics, location, and polarity to interpret citation relationships.
limitations: Review, not causal; does not address LLMs.
relevance_to_our_project: high - supports moving from raw citation counts to citation-meaning quality
notes: Key basis for adding citation-function accuracy to the health standard.

title: What do citation counts measure? A review of studies on citing behavior
topic: Citing behavior and meaning of citation counts
data_source: Empirical studies on citing behavior from early 1960s-mid-2005
key_variables: citing motivations; intellectual influence; non-scientific factors; citation counts
key_findings: Finds citing behavior is not driven only by intellectual or cognitive influence; social and non-scientific motives also affect citation decisions.
limitations: Pre-LLM; review period ends before current open-science and AI era.
relevance_to_our_project: high - foundational caution for interpreting citation counts
notes: Useful for arguing healthy citations require attention to motive and function, not just volume.

title: Citation Context Analysis as a Method for Conducting Rigorous and Impactful Literature Reviews
authors: Marc H. Anderson and Russell K. Lemken
source_type: keyword search; venue search; conceptual expansion
topic: Citation context analysis for literature review and theory development
data_source: Citation contexts in organizational studies and broader science
method: methodological article; qualitative/quantitative citation context analysis
key_variables: citation context; knowledge claims; empirical testing; critique; realized impact
key_findings: Argues citation context analysis can reveal how ideas are used, tested, critiqued, and transformed, going beyond raw citation counts.
limitations: Methodological rather than large-scale empirical; not LLM-specific.
relevance_to_our_project: high - business/management method for citation health and meaning
gap_category: business venue; citation context; system health
notes: Directly relevant to management/business framing and to measuring healthy citation as meaningful uptake.

title: Understanding the meanings of citations using sentiment, role, and citation function classifications
topic: Automated classification of citation meaning
data_source: Indonesian journal articles in five science areas
key_variables: citation sentiment; citation role; citation function; citation location
key_findings: Shows citation meaning can be classified by sentiment, role, and function; many citations are used for introductions or relation-building rather than comparison or substantive use.
limitations: Specific corpus; classification categories and field coverage may not generalize.
relevance_to_our_project: medium - operationalizes citation-function quality for future LLM citation studies
notes: Useful for measuring whether LLM-influenced citations are substantive or ornamental.

title: The extent and drivers of gender imbalance in neuroscience reference lists
topic: Gender imbalance in citation practices
data_source: Reference lists from five top neuroscience journals
level_of_analysis: citation level; author-demographic level; journal level
key_variables: author gender; reference list composition; citation imbalance; citing author gender
key_findings: Finds neuroscience reference lists over-cite papers with men as first and last authors relative to expectation; imbalance is largely driven by men and increased as the field diversified.
limitations: Gender inference limitations; field-specific; focuses gender rather than other axes of epistemic exclusion.
relevance_to_our_project: high - demonstrates citation health includes inclusion and fair uptake, not only relevance
notes: Supports revising fair opportunity standard toward measured representational and epistemic justice.

title: What Is the Harm in Gendered Citation Practices?
topic: Epistemic harm and gendered citation practices
data_source: Philosophy of science and feminist epistemology
key_variables: gendered citation; participatory epistemic injustice; uptake; cumulative harm
key_findings: Argues gendered citation practices are participatory epistemic injustice that harms individual scientists and scientific communities by limiting uptake.
limitations: Conceptual; not LLM-specific; gender focus only.
relevance_to_our_project: high - provides normative foundation for citation justice and ecosystem health
notes: Strengthens health standard: fair citation is about community epistemic capacity, not just individual credit.

title: Automatic classification of citation function
authors: Simone Teufel, Advaith Siddharthan and Dan Tidhar
topic: Citation function classification
data_source: Scientific paper citation contexts
key_variables: citation function; citation context; rhetorical role

title: Citation manipulation through citation mills and pre-print servers

level_of_analysis: researcher level; citation level; platform level
key_variables: citation counts; citation manipulation; citation boosting; citation mills; Google Scholar
key_findings: Shows citation counts are widely used and can create incentives to game the system through self-citations, cartels, coercive citation, and citation mills; discusses difficulty distinguishing legitimate from manipulative citations.

gap_category: citation ethics; responsible metrics; system health
